title: Why Homework Should Be Abolished
text: My younger brother started getting a full two hours of homework every night this year, and his grades actually went down compared to last year. That alone shows homework does not help students learn — if anything it just makes them tired and less interested in school. Every classroom I have ever been in worked better when the teacher explained things well and let us practice at school, not at home. Schools should scrap homework completely and trust that classroom time is enough for every student to master the material.
embedded_errors: Draws a sweeping causal conclusion ('homework does not help students learn') from a single anecdotal case; ignores confounding explanations for the sibling's grade drop; generalizes from personal classroom experience to a universal policy recommendation without addressing the mixed research literature on homework effectiveness.

title: The Ozone Layer and Global Warming
text: The ozone layer plays a bigger role in climate change than people usually realize, since a thinner ozone layer lets more solar radiation reach the surface and adds to the warming trend. This is part of why global temperatures have climbed over the same decades that the ozone hole was largest. The Montreal Protocol's work to repair the ozone layer should therefore help slow warming somewhat, even though greenhouse gases remain the main driver overall.
embedded_errors: Overstates ozone depletion's actual contribution to surface warming relative to greenhouse gases, whose effect is far larger.|Implies a stronger causal/temporal link between the size of the ozone hole and global temperature trends than the science supports; the two are driven by largely separate atmospheric mechanisms.

title: How Much of the Brain Do We Really Use
text: Brain scans show that at any given moment, only a small fraction of your neurons are actively firing, which is why the old idea that we use 'only 10 percent of the brain' captures something real even if the number itself is a myth. Most of the brain really is sitting idle most of the time, waiting for the right task to switch it on. This is why intense mental training, like chess or music, can supposedly activate regions that an average person's brain rarely touches at all.
embedded_errors: Misrepresents normal neural activity: different regions are active for different tasks across a day, but essentially the whole brain is used over any typical 24-hour period, not 'sitting idle'.|The myth is not partially true; imaging studies do not support the claim that untrained people leave large brain regions permanently unused.

title: Human Origins
text: Humans evolved directly from modern chimpanzees, which is why the two species look so similar. Evolution always moves towards greater complexity, and humans are its final product. Chimpanzees that survive today are simply the ones that failed to evolve. Darwin himself described this process as the survival of the strongest.
embedded_errors: Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor; neither evolved from the other.|Evolution is not directional and has no final product; 'survival of the fittest' was coined by Spencer and does not mean 'strongest'.

title: Why IQ Tests Should Be Ignored Completely
text: I know someone who scored low on an IQ test in school but went on to build a very successful business, which proves IQ tests don't measure anything that actually matters in real life. If a test can't predict something as important as career success in a single case, it isn't worth giving to anyone. Schools and employers should stop using IQ scores altogether and rely only on interviews and personal impressions instead, since those give a much fuller picture of a person's real ability.
embedded_errors: Generalizes from one counterexample to a blanket dismissal of IQ testing's validity; ignores that IQ scores are population-level statistical predictors, not guarantees about individual outcomes; the proposed alternative is asserted to be more reliable with no supporting reasoning, when unstructured interviews are well known to be a weaker predictor.

title: How Electric Current Travels Through a Wire
text: When you flip a switch, the signal that turns the lamp on travels through the wire almost as fast as light, so in everyday terms it's fair to say electricity itself moves through copper at close to light speed. This near-instant transmission is what makes electrical circuits so much faster than, say, water flowing through a pipe. Because the whole wire responds almost simultaneously, thicker wires don't really change how quickly a device switches on — they only matter for how much current the wire can safely carry.
embedded_errors: Blurs the distinction between the electromagnetic field/signal, which does propagate near light speed, and the actual drift velocity of electrons (millimetres per second) — saying 'electricity itself moves... at close to light speed' treats these as the same thing, a common but technically incorrect simplification.

title: Vitamin C and the Common Cold
text: Taking vitamin C regularly is one of the best-supported ways to protect yourself from getting a cold in the first place, and most nutrition guides recommend it for exactly this reason. Once you do catch a cold, upping your vitamin C intake at the first sign of symptoms can meaningfully shorten how long you're sick. Because of this, keeping vitamin C levels high through the winter is generally considered a solid, low-effort way to cut down on the number of colds you get each year.
embedded_errors: Overstates the evidence: for the general population, regular vitamin C supplementation has not been shown to meaningfully reduce cold incidence (large trials find no significant prevention effect except in specific groups like endurance athletes).|The modest reduction in cold duration seen in some studies is much smaller than implied and is not evidence of a strong protective/preventive effect.

title: The Tallest Mountain
text: Mount Everest, at 8,849 metres, is the tallest mountain on Earth by every measure that scientists use. Nothing on the planet rises higher from its base, and no other summit is farther from the centre of the Earth. Everest grows about one metre per year as India pushes into Asia, which means it will overtake the height of the atmosphere within a few thousand years.
embedded_errors: Mauna Kea is taller measured from base to summit; Chimborazo's summit is farthest from Earth's centre.|Everest rises a few millimetres per year, not one metre, and will not approach the height of the atmosphere.

title: Why Statistics Can Prove Almost Anything
text: I once saw two studies on the same topic reach completely opposite conclusions, which tells you that statistics as a method is basically unreliable and can be twisted to support whatever the researcher wants. If experts using the same tools can disagree that much, ordinary people should just trust their own common sense over any statistical study. That's why I generally ignore headlines that say 'studies show,' since in my experience the numbers behind them can always be spun either way.
embedded_errors: Draws a sweeping conclusion about the entire discipline of statistics from a single instance of conflicting findings, without considering identifiable causes of disagreement (sample size, methodology, confounders); recommends trusting 'common sense' over statistical evidence without justification.

title: Where Nepali's Vocabulary Comes From
text: Nepali's vocabulary is overwhelmingly Sanskrit in origin, which is why it feels so close to Hindi and other North Indian languages that share the same Sanskrit-heavy base. Because of this shared vocabulary base, a fluent Hindi speaker can generally follow spoken Nepali with only a little extra effort, even without ever having studied it formally. This close relationship is part of why some linguists have historically debated whether Nepali is best described as its own language or a closely related dialect within the broader Hindi language family.
embedded_errors: Overstates the closeness: Nepali also has substantial vocabulary from Tibeto-Burman and other regional sources, not just Sanskrit, and mutual intelligibility with Hindi is considerably more limited than implied.|Nepali is classified as a distinct language in the Pahari subgroup of Indo-Aryan, not a dialect within a 'Hindi language family,' and this is not a live linguistic debate today.

title: Napoleon's Final Years
text: After his defeat at Waterloo in 1815, Napoleon was captured by a coalition that was led mainly by the British, and he was quickly exiled to the island of Saint Helena, where he lived under guard until his death in 1821. Because Napoleon lost so decisively, his legal reforms were dismantled soon afterward and had little lasting influence outside France itself. His military career is generally remembered as a story of early brilliance followed by a final, complete failure that left behind no significant legacy.
embedded_errors: Understates the coalition's composition: Prussian forces under Blücher were essential to the Waterloo victory, not just the British.|Significantly understates the Napoleonic Code's lasting impact, which shaped civil law across large parts of Europe well after his defeat, contradicting the claim of little lasting influence.

title: Why We Have Seasons
text: Earth's orbit is a strong ellipse, and we have summer when we are closest to the Sun and winter when we are farthest away. This is why summer arrives at the same time everywhere on Earth. The Moon's gravity also tilts the planet a little each year, which is what makes some summers hotter than others.
embedded_errors: Seasons are caused by axial tilt, not orbital distance; the hemispheres have opposite seasons.|The Moon stabilises Earth's tilt rather than changing it year to year; it does not cause interannual temperature variation this way.

title: Why Phones Should Never Be Allowed in Schools
text: At my cousin's school, they banned phones completely last year and everyone says the students seem happier now, so that settles it — phones are clearly bad for students and every school should ban them outright. Kids today spend so much time looking at screens that it's obvious this is hurting their ability to focus in class. Any school still allowing phones during the day is choosing convenience over its students' wellbeing, plain and simple.
embedded_errors: Relies on secondhand, anecdotal impressions ('everyone says') from a single school as proof of a general causal claim; treats a correlational, subjectively reported mood change as settling a complex empirical question; frames schools that allow phones as careless without engaging any counterarguments (emergency contact, accessibility, digital literacy).

title: Why Nepal Should Scrap the Provincial System
text: Since federalism began, my home district hasn't seen any new roads or hospitals, so it's clear the whole provincial system was a waste of money from day one. All that federalism really did was create extra layers of ministers, offices and salaries that add cost without adding any real benefit to ordinary people. Nepal was better off under a single central government, and going back to that system would immediately fix the problems people are dealing with today.
embedded_errors: Generalizes from one district's experience to a judgment about the entire federal system nationwide; treats absent infrastructure in one area as proof federalism itself failed, ignoring other explanations (implementation gaps, budget execution, time since restructuring); asserts reverting to a unitary system would 'immediately fix' problems with no supporting argument.

title: How Nepal's Current Constitution Came About
text: Nepal's current constitution was promulgated in September 2015, a little over seven years after the country was declared a republic, following a Constituent Assembly process that had already produced a draft once before under an earlier Assembly. The new charter formally established Nepal as a federal republic with seven provinces, replacing the earlier unitary structure inherited from before 2008. Because the drafting process spanned two separate Constituent Assemblies, the final document is often described as the product of nearly a decade of constitutional negotiation.
embedded_errors: Nepal was declared a republic in May 2008 and the constitution promulgated in September 2015 — the roughly seven-year gap is correct, but the passage presents the process as smoothly consensual and omits that the 2015 promulgation was heavily contested at the time, particularly by Madhes-based parties.

title: How a Bill Becomes Law in Nepal
text: In Nepal's federal parliament, most bills need to pass through both the House of Representatives and the National Assembly, and the National Assembly's approval is generally treated as a formality since it rarely amends or delays legislation that the House has already passed. Once both houses have approved a bill, it goes to the President for authentication before becoming law. Money bills are a partial exception, since they originate only in the House of Representatives, though the National Assembly still reviews them before they proceed.
embedded_errors: Understates the National Assembly's role by calling it 'generally... a formality' — it actively debates, can amend, and can return non-money bills to the House.|Overstates its role on money bills: the National Assembly cannot approve or block them, only offer opinions within a fixed period, after which the bill proceeds regardless.

title: Citizenship Rules in Nepal
text: Nepal has long allowed its citizens to freely hold dual citizenship with any country they choose, a policy unchanged since the country's founding. Citizenship by descent is granted only through the father's line, and children of a Nepali mother and foreign father cannot acquire Nepali citizenship under any circumstance. There is no separate identity card for non-resident Nepalis, since they are treated as full dual citizens automatically.
embedded_errors: Nepal follows a single-citizenship policy and does not generally allow dual citizenship for its citizens.|The constitution provides pathways for citizenship by descent through the mother as well, not the father's line only.|Non-resident Nepalis can obtain a distinct NRN identity card, which is not full citizenship, contradicting the claim that they are treated as automatic dual citizens.

title: Why Local Governments Shouldn't Handle Big Budgets
text: My local ward spent its whole development budget on a park nobody uses instead of fixing the road everyone actually needed, which shows local governments simply can't be trusted to spend money wisely. If a small ward can get its priorities that wrong, imagine how badly bigger municipalities are wasting their budgets too. All major spending decisions should be sent back up to the federal government, since only they have the experience to decide what a community actually needs.
embedded_errors: Generalizes from one ward's poor spending decision to a blanket claim about local governments nationwide; assumes bigger municipalities waste money too based on a single small example; asserts the federal government has superior insight into local needs with no supporting reasoning, undercutting the basic rationale for devolving budget authority.

title: How Nepal Taxes Goods and Services
text: Nepal's standard VAT rate is 13 percent, applied broadly across most goods and services sold in the country, which puts Nepal roughly in line with VAT rates seen elsewhere in South Asia. Because VAT is charged at each stage of production and resale, the final consumer effectively pays a cumulative tax that can end up noticeably higher than the headline 13 percent rate by the time a product reaches the shelf. This is one reason VAT is often criticized as a hidden tax that quietly raises prices more than the sticker rate suggests.
embedded_errors: Misrepresents how VAT works: businesses can claim credit for VAT already paid at earlier stages, so the tax does not stack cumulatively across the supply chain — the final consumer pays approximately the headline rate on final value, not a compounded multiple, which is what distinguishes VAT from a cascading turnover tax.

title: How Judges Are Appointed in Nepal
text: Nepal's judiciary operates through three tiers — district courts, high courts, and the Supreme Court — and judges at all three levels are appointed directly by the President without needing recommendation from any other constitutional body. The Chief Justice, once appointed, effectively serves for life, since there is no fixed retirement age written into the constitution. This structure is meant to keep the judiciary fully independent of the legislature and executive alike.
embedded_errors: Judicial appointments go through the Judicial Council, which recommends appointees for the President to formally appoint — the President does not appoint judges directly without this recommendation.|Nepal's constitution sets a mandatory retirement age for judges (65 for Supreme Court judges), so the Chief Justice does not serve for life.

title: Nepal's Electoral System
text: Every member of Nepal's House of Representatives is elected purely through proportional representation, with no directly contested constituency seats at all. The National Assembly, similarly, is elected entirely by ordinary citizens through direct popular vote nationwide.
embedded_errors: The House of Representatives uses a mixed system: 165 seats by first-past-the-post and 110 by proportional representation, not proportional representation alone.|The National Assembly is elected indirectly, mainly by an electoral college of local and provincial representatives, not by direct nationwide popular vote.

title: Why Nepal's Civil Service Exams Should Be Scrapped
text: I know someone who scored extremely well on the Lok Sewa exam but turned out to be a terrible, disorganized officer once they actually started working, which proves the exam doesn't test anything that matters for the job. If a written test can produce an outcome like that, the whole exam-based hiring system is clearly broken and should be replaced. Nepal should just let ministries hire and promote staff based on interviews and direct recommendations instead, since that would obviously do a better job of finding capable officers.
embedded_errors: Generalizes from a single anecdotal case to a conclusion about the validity of the entire examination system; ignores that a written exam tests general knowledge and aptitude rather than guaranteeing performance; proposes replacing exams with interviews and recommendations without acknowledging the well-documented nepotism/inconsistency risk exams were introduced to reduce.

title: Nepal's Anti-Corruption Commission
text: The Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA) is Nepal's main constitutional body for tackling corruption, and its investigations can lead directly to the removal of any government employee found guilty, including elected officials such as ministers and members of parliament. Because its mandate covers essentially the entire public sector, the CIAA is often described as having the final word on corruption cases in Nepal, with no further appeal process once it reaches a decision. This broad, largely unchecked authority is part of why the CIAA is considered one of the most powerful constitutional bodies in the country.
embedded_errors: Overstates the CIAA's authority: it does not have unilateral removal power over elected officials such as ministers or MPs, whose accountability runs through separate constitutional/parliamentary processes.|CIAA decisions are not final and unappealable — they can be challenged in court, including the Supreme Court, contradicting the claim of 'no further appeal process.'
